You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

steps.text:
No demo pairs yet. Request one.

The test input shows scattered 6s on a background of 0s, but the transformation rule isn't clear from a single input. I'll ask for a demonstration pair to learn how the output is derived.

Demo: 6s and 5s. The transformation fills in pattern: where there's a gap between two 5s in a row, fill with alternating 2s? Let me parse: each row of input has 5s at some positions; output replaces... Actually look at row 0: "6 6 ... 5 6 5 6 ..." becomes "... 5 2 5". So the rule: between two 5s separated by exactly one 6, that 6 becomes 2. Check row 1: 5 at col 11, then 6 at 12, 5 at 13 → 6→2. Then 5,6,5 → 2. Yes: single 6 between two 5s becomes 2. Row 9: 5s at cols 3..17 alternating, pairs 5-6-5 → middle becomes 2.

Wait but is it always single-gap? All examples seem single gaps only. Apply to test input: 0s are background (no 5s), so only 6s matter. In test, rows have isolated 6s, never two 5s adjacent... no 5s present! Test has only 0 and 6. Hmm — so test would be unchanged? That seems odd. Maybe rule applies to both colors generally: pairs of same color with one cell between become filled with 2. But test has no 5s, so output = input? Possible but suspicious. Check test: e.g. row 1: 6 at col2, then 0, then 6 at col4 — 0 between two 6s → should become 2? But demo shows only 5s paired. With no other info, safest: transform any single-cell gap between two equal non-zero cells into 2? Demo consistent. Test: 6 at (1,2), 0 at (1,3), 6 at (1,4) → 0 becomes 2. Also row 0: 6 at 1, 0 at 2, 6 at 3 → 2. Row 2 all zero. Row 3: 6s at 0,2,4,6 → 0s at 1,3,5 → 2. Etc.

Apply f: for each cell, if neighbors left and right exist and equal nonzero, set to 2. Check demo consistency quickly mentally — yes matches.

Let me code and verify against demo, then submit test transformed.
